title: Camera and IMU measurement models
summary: Camera observations, inertial measurements, and their roles in six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) motion estimation.
objectives: Distinguish image observations from inertial measurements
Explain why an accelerometer does not directly measure position
Separate local odometry from globally corrected SLAM

sections.title: Camera and inertial measurements
body: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) estimates six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) motion: three position and three orientation degrees of freedom. A camera supplies image observations. A gyroscope measures angular velocity, and an accelerometer measures specific force. These measurements constrain a navigation state that also includes velocity and sensor biases.

In a calibrated pinhole model, a point with camera coordinates (x, y, z) projects to normalized coordinates (x/z, y/z). One image therefore provides a bearing, not an independent depth measurement. Observations across images relate scene geometry to camera motion; camera intrinsics then connect normalized coordinates to pixels.

sources.title: OpenVINS: camera measurement model
Guoquan Huang: Visual-Inertial Navigation: A Concise Review (2019), Sections 2–3

sections.title: Specific force and the gravity convention
body: Let G denote the local global frame and I the IMU frame. R_IG maps vectors from G to I. Following OpenVINS, define g_G = [0, 0, g]ᵀ with g approximately 9.81 m/s²; physical gravitational acceleration is −g_G. Let a_G be the IMU origin’s physical acceleration expressed in G. The model below assumes that IMU scale and axis-misalignment effects have already been corrected.

The measured specific force a_m, accelerometer bias b_a, and noise n_a are expressed in I, in m/s². A stationary sensor ideally reads R_IG g_G. Rotating the bias-corrected reading into G and subtracting g_G recovers physical acceleration. A fixed subtraction along one sensor axis is incorrect when the sensor rotates.

sources.title: OpenVINS: IMU propagation derivations

sections.equation: a_m = R_IG (a_G + g_G) + b_a + n_a; a_G = R_IGᵀ (a_m − b_a − n_a) − g_G
sections.equationLatex: \begin{aligned}\mathbf a_m &= \mathbf R_{IG}(\mathbf a_G+\mathbf g_G)+\mathbf b_a+\mathbf n_a\\ \mathbf a_G &= \mathbf R_{IG}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf a_m-\mathbf b_a-\mathbf n_a)-\mathbf g_G\end{aligned}

sections.title: Inertial propagation and visual updates
body: For the calibrated gyroscope model, ω_m = ω_I + b_g + n_g, with angular velocity and bias in rad/s. IMU integration propagates orientation, velocity, and position between visual updates; bias and noise produce accumulating errors. Image measurements constrain this propagation through the camera model.

Monocular visual–inertial estimation can recover metric scale under sufficiently informative motion and appropriate calibration. This is not guaranteed for every trajectory. Weak image geometry, uninformative motion, or incorrect timing can leave the estimate poorly constrained.

sources.title: OpenVINS: IMU propagation derivations
Guoquan Huang: Visual-Inertial Navigation: A Concise Review (2019), Sections 2–3

sections.title: Odometry and map correction
body: Local odometry can accumulate drift. Visual–inertial SLAM may additionally use mapped landmarks, loop closures, or prior-map information to constrain long-term estimates. Retaining some feature states does not by itself establish a global loop-closure capability. For evaluation, identify the output trajectory and whether global corrections were applied.

exercise.question: A stationary, level IMU reports approximately 9.81 m/s² on its upward axis. Does this imply upward motion?
exercise.answer: No. Ignoring bias and noise, the reading is specific force. Under this lesson’s OpenVINS convention, R_IGᵀ a_m − g_G is zero at rest. The symbol g_G denotes [0, 0, g]ᵀ; the physical gravitational acceleration is −g_G.

title: Coordinate frames and pose conventions
summary: Global, IMU, and camera frames; rigid-transform direction; and the OpenVINS JPL quaternion convention.
objectives: Read the source and destination of a rigid transform
Invert and compose transforms correctly
Distinguish quaternion algebra, component order, and rotation direction
Identify the physical frame represented by a trajectory

sections.title: Frame labels and axes
body: G denotes a local global frame, I an IMU frame, and C a camera frame. R_AB maps vector coordinates from B to A; this is the destination–source convention used throughout these lessons. OpenVINS writes the global-to-IMU rotation as ᴵ_G R and stores the corresponding quaternion together with the IMU position expressed in G.

A frame label does not specify its axes. ROS body frames commonly use x forward, y left, z up, while optical frames use x right, y down, z forward. Check the actual dataset and sensor definitions. Positions and translations here use meters, and angles use radians unless stated otherwise.

sources.title: OpenVINS: filter state, sensor frames, and time offset
ROS REP 103: units and coordinate conventions

sections.title: Rigid transforms and composition
body: T_AB maps a point from B to A. Its translation t_AB is the position of B’s origin expressed in A. Kalibr’s T_cam_imu is T_CI: it maps IMU coordinates into camera coordinates. This matches OpenVINS camera extrinsics R_ItoC and p_IinC.

To map a camera point into G, use T_GC = T_GI T_IC, with the rightmost transform acting first. Invert T_CI to obtain T_IC. An inverse requires a transposed rotation and a rotated negative translation; negating translation alone is generally incorrect.

sections.equation: p_A = R_AB p_B + t_AB; T_BA = [R_ABᵀ, −R_ABᵀ t_AB; 0, 1]
sections.equationLatex: \mathbf p_A=\mathbf R_{AB}\mathbf p_B+\mathbf t_{AB},\qquad \mathbf T_{BA}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf R_{AB}^{\mathsf T}&-\mathbf R_{AB}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf t_{AB}\\\mathbf 0^{\mathsf T}&1\end{bmatrix}

sections.title: JPL quaternion convention
body: OpenVINS uses a unit JPL quaternion q̄ = [q_vᵀ, q₄]ᵀ, with three vector components followed by the scalar. Component order alone is insufficient: its algebra has ij = −k, whereas Hamilton algebra has ij = k. This algebraic convention does not change the handedness of the coordinate frames.

The equation gives the OpenVINS rotation matrix, with [q_v]× v = q_v × v. For the IMU state it represents R_IG, from G to I. OpenVINS uses a left-multiplicative orientation error: q̄ = δq̄ ⊗ q̄_hat. Conversion to another library must preserve the intended rotation direction and algebra; merely reordering four numbers is insufficient. A known-vector rotation and its inverse provide useful checks.

sources.title: OpenVINS: JPL quaternion definition and perturbation
OpenVINS: quaternion and rigid-transform operations

sections.equationLatex: \mathbf R(\bar q)=(2q_4^2-1)\mathbf I_3-2q_4[\mathbf q_v]_\times+2\mathbf q_v\mathbf q_v^{\mathsf T},\qquad \|\bar q\|=1

sections.title: Trajectory reference frame
body: A trajectory may track the IMU, camera, or ground-truth marker. Their separated origins follow different position paths during rotation. Apply the known rigid transform so estimates and references describe the same physical frame. Also record whether the output uses a locally continuous odometry frame or a globally corrected map frame.

exercise.question: If T_GI maps IMU coordinates into G and T_IC maps camera coordinates into I, how is a camera point mapped into G?
exercise.answer: T_GC = T_GI T_IC. Apply T_IC first and T_GI second. If calibration instead supplies T_CI, invert it before composition.

title: Camera–IMU calibration and synchronization
summary: Spatial calibration, clock offsets, IMU noise parameters, and the motion conditions needed to estimate them.
objectives: Separate deterministic calibration parameters from stochastic noise parameters
Interpret the camera–IMU time-offset sign
Recognize motion-dependent calibration observability
Check noise units and calibration evidence

sections.title: Calibration quantities
body: Camera intrinsics specify projection and distortion. Camera–IMU extrinsics specify the rigid sensor transform. IMU intrinsics model effects such as scale errors and axis misalignment; these are distinct from measurement-noise and bias-evolution parameters. Temporal calibration relates camera and IMU timestamps. The active model determines which quantities are fixed and which are estimated.

Calibration must match the input images. Cropping, resizing, rectification, or a changed camera mode can alter the relation between pixels and rays. Retain the image geometry, sensor settings, and processing steps with the calibration.

sources.title: OpenVINS: sensor calibration and report inspection
Yang, Geneva, Zuo, and Huang, Online Self-Calibration for Visual-Inertial Navigation: Models, Analysis, and Degeneracy (T-RO 2023)

sections.title: Time-offset convention
body: OpenVINS and Kalibr define the offset in seconds by t_imu = t_cam + t_off. Kalibr names it timeshift_cam_imu. Thus a positive offset maps an image timestamp to a later value on the IMU clock. Software using another definition may require a sign conversion.

Timestamps should consistently describe acquisition time. Message-arrival times can include buffering and transport delays. Inspect missing samples, duplicate timestamps, jumps, and irregular intervals. A constant offset cannot correct arbitrary timing jitter or a wrong time unit.

Kalibr: camera–IMU calibration procedure

sections.title: Motion excitation and calibration evidence
body: For target-based camera–IMU calibration, keep the target stationary and move the rigid sensor assembly through varied orientations and translations while preserving target visibility and limiting blur. Review image and IMU residuals, timestamp intervals, and the recovered transform’s physical plausibility. Repeatability across recordings provides additional evidence.

Yang, Geneva, Zuo, and Huang’s full self-calibration analysis establishes calibration observability under fully excited six-axis motion for the studied model. Degenerate motions can leave particular parameters unobservable. This condition is model-specific: optimizer convergence, or motion around one axis, does not establish that every calibration parameter was identified. Online refinement also requires informative measurements.

sections.title: Continuous and discrete noise
body: In the Kalibr/OpenVINS model, gyroscope and accelerometer white-noise densities have units (rad/s)/√Hz and (m/s²)/√Hz. The corresponding bias-driving random-walk densities have units (rad/s²)/√Hz and (m/s³)/√Hz. These are different quantities from a per-sample measurement standard deviation.

For sample interval Δt in seconds, the idealized model below maps a gyroscope noise density σ_g to a discrete measurement standard deviation σ_g,d. The bias increment standard deviation σ_bg,d scales differently. Analogous expressions hold for the accelerometer. The white-noise conversion assumes appropriate filtering and sampling; simply discarding samples does not establish those assumptions. Preserve the characterization procedure and sensor filtering settings.

title: VIO initialization
summary: The initial navigation state, stationary and dynamic startup assumptions, and limits imposed by observability.
objectives: Distinguish 6-DoF pose from the IMU navigation state and its error coordinates
Identify stationary and dynamic initialization assumptions
Explain the unobservable global position and yaw
Separate startup failure from subsequent tracking loss

sections.title: Initial state and uncertainty
body: The OpenVINS IMU state contains a global-to-IMU unit quaternion, IMU position and velocity in G, and gyroscope and accelerometer biases. It stores 16 scalar entries, but its local error state has 15 dimensions: three orientation errors and four three-component vector errors. The 6-DoF pose is only part of this state. Cloned poses, features, and estimated calibration parameters enlarge the complete filter state.

Initialization provides estimates and their uncertainty. For visual–inertial estimation without global references, three global translations and rotation about gravity are unobservable under generic, sufficiently informative motion. Degenerate motion may introduce further unobservable directions. Setting an initial position and yaw chooses a coordinate convention; it does not obtain absolute position or heading from the sensors.

sources.title: OpenVINS: IMU state and 15-dimensional error update
OpenVINS: filter state, sensor frames, and time offset
OpenVINS: VINS observability and consistency

sections.equation: x_I = [q̄_IGᵀ, p_I_Gᵀ, v_I_Gᵀ, b_gᵀ, b_aᵀ]ᵀ; dim(δx_I) = 15
sections.equationLatex: \mathbf x_I=\begin{bmatrix}\bar q_{IG}^{\mathsf T}&({}^{G}\mathbf p_I)^{\mathsf T}&({}^{G}\mathbf v_I)^{\mathsf T}&\mathbf b_g^{\mathsf T}&\mathbf b_a^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T},\qquad \dim(\delta\mathbf x_I)=15

sections.title: Stationary initialization
body: A stationary interval supports gravity alignment and gyroscope-bias estimation when its assumptions hold. OpenVINS uses an earlier stationary window and can require a subsequent acceleration change before starting. It initializes zero velocity and position, obtains orientation from average acceleration, and assigns biases consistently with that choice.

One static orientation cannot independently identify arbitrary accelerometer bias and tilt. Small measurement variation also does not prove zero motion: constant velocity or constant acceleration with unchanged orientation can produce steady IMU readings. Gravity constrains tilt under the stationary assumptions; it does not determine yaw.

sources.title: OpenVINS: static initialization assumptions
OpenVINS: static initialization implementation

sections.title: Dynamic initialization
body: Geneva and Huang’s OpenVINS initialization report combines feature tracks with inertial preintegration over a time window. An initial solve in the first IMU frame estimates velocity, gravity direction, and feature geometry subject to known gravity magnitude. Nonlinear maximum-likelihood refinement then improves the state, with covariance recovery for the estimator that follows.

The initial construction uses supplied bias values and assumes camera calibration and camera–IMU extrinsics are reasonably accurate. Subsequent refinement does not guarantee recovery from arbitrary calibration errors. A short startup interval may not sufficiently constrain all calibration parameters. Weak parallax, interrupted tracks, or poorly excited motion can prevent a well-conditioned solution; faster movement can also increase blur.

sources.title: Patrick Geneva and Guoquan Huang: OpenVINS State Initialization: Details and Derivations, RPNG-2022-INIT, updated February 2023
OpenVINS: dynamic initialization procedure

sections.title: Initialization diagnostics
body: Check delivery of both sensor streams, timestamp units and offset, calibration, and the chosen startup interval. Inspect feature tracks, initialization status, and the first estimated state. Record when initialization succeeds so a failure to start is distinguished from later tracking loss.

Preserve the original recording. When testing a different start time or assumption, record the interval and configuration. A successful return from the initializer is evidence of completing that procedure, not independent verification of calibration or subsequent trajectory accuracy.

exercise.question: Why can a gravity-aligned stationary IMU still have arbitrary initial yaw?
exercise.answer: A rotation about the gravity direction leaves the stationary gravity observation unchanged. Gravity alignment therefore cannot identify yaw. Without a heading reference, an initial yaw is a local coordinate choice.

title: Filtering and optimization
summary: Understand how retained states, feature elimination, and linearization choices connect filtering and sliding-window optimization.
objectives: Identify the IMU state, pose clones, and optional landmark states in OpenVINS
Explain feature elimination at a fixed linearization point
Describe why marginalization and FEJ require compatible linearization choices

sections.title: Start with a probabilistic estimation problem
body: A visual residual compares a measured feature location with its prediction. IMU measurements support propagation in an EKF or motion factors in a batch formulation. Under a conditionally independent Gaussian factor model with fixed covariances, a maximum a posteriori estimate combines a prior with covariance-weighted inertial and visual residuals. A residual covariance is not the posterior state covariance.

The schematic objective below includes the prior in the residual index. Rotations require local perturbations rather than ordinary vector addition. Robust losses, outlier rejection, and which measurements are retained are additional design choices. The estimator family alone does not specify these choices.

sources.title: Chen, Geneva, Peng, Lee, and Huang, Optimization-based VINS: Consistency, Marginalization, and FEJ (IROS 2023)
Geneva et al., OpenVINS: A Research Platform for Visual-Inertial Estimation (ICRA 2020)

sections.equation: x* = arg min_x (1/2) Σ_i r_i(x)ᵀ Σ_i⁻¹ r_i(x)

sections.title: An MSCKF retains correlated pose clones
body: OpenVINS maintains the current IMU orientation, position, velocity, and biases, together with selected past IMU pose clones. These clones retain orientation and position, not a complete historical IMU state at every image. Their cross-covariances let visual constraints on past poses update the correlated current state.

An MSCKF feature is triangulated for the measurement update and eliminated from the linearized constraint; it need not become a persistent landmark state. OpenVINS can additionally retain SLAM landmarks and estimate selected calibration parameters. Report the enabled state variables and clone/landmark limits for the configuration being compared.

sources.title: OpenVINS: retained state variables
Geneva et al., OpenVINS: A Research Platform for Visual-Inertial Estimation (ICRA 2020)
OpenVINS: MSCKF nullspace projection

sections.title: Eliminate the feature, retain its motion constraint
body: For one track, the stacked linearized residual depends on retained-state error δx and feature-position error δp_f. A basis N for the left nullspace of H_f removes the feature term. The projected noise covariance must also be carried into the update; projecting the residual does not make its uncertainty disappear.

For the same whitened linear least-squares system, eliminating an unconstrained feature by an orthonormal nullspace projection or by a Schur complement gives the same reduced quadratic in the retained variables when the whitened feature Jacobian has full column rank. This is a conditional algebraic equivalence. Different priors, measurements, linearization points, or later relinearization produce different estimation problems.

sources.title: OpenVINS: MSCKF nullspace projection

Yang, Maley, and Huang, Null-Space-based Marginalization: Analysis and Algorithm (IROS 2017)

sections.equation: r ≈ H_x δx + H_f δp_f + n; NᵀH_f = 0 ⇒ Nᵀr ≈ NᵀH_x δx + Nᵀn

sections.title: Marginalization fixes part of the linearization history
body: A sliding-window optimizer can repeatedly linearize active nonlinear factors. Removing old variables usually replaces their factors with a quadratic prior at the marginalization linearization point. That prior preserves the eliminated linearized information; it does not preserve the ability to relinearize the original nonlinear measurements.

For ordinary VIO under sufficiently informative motion and without an external global reference, global translation and rotation about gravity remain unobservable. Incompatible linearizations can falsely add information in these directions. FEJ uses designated first estimates in the relevant Jacobians to preserve the intended nullspace; it does not freeze the estimated trajectory. Chen et al. show that its application in optimization depends on the marginalization structure and connected factors.

body: Compare camera mode, input rate and resolution, active states, track lengths, landmark counts, calibration settings, solver iterations, and linearization policy. Accuracy and computation must be measured under documented conditions; they do not follow from the labels filtering and optimization alone.

exercise.answer: No. The input and configuration differences also change computational work. First compare a documented common condition, then vary one setting to study its effect.

title: Trajectory error and evaluation coverage
summary: Understand ATE, RPE, alignment, and why an error number needs an explicit evaluation interval and denominator.
objectives: Distinguish single-run error, repeated-run summaries, and dataset aggregation
Specify pose association, alignment, and RPE pair conventions
Separate evaluated extent, local valid-path fraction, and execution outcomes

sections.title: Establish corresponding poses and output semantics
body: Compare the same physical sensor frame using a declared pose direction, quaternion convention, position units, and timestamp units. Specify timestamp association, tolerance, interpolation, and the valid reference intervals. Converting a text layout does not apply the camera-to-IMU or marker-to-IMU transform.

Record whether the trajectory contains estimates produced online at each timestamp, states revised by a smoother, or poses corrected by loop closure. OpenVINS recommends collecting the current estimate when evaluating online estimator behavior. These outputs should not be silently mixed in a comparison.

sources.title: OpenVINS: recording and evaluating estimator outputs
Zhang and Scaramuzza, A Tutorial on Quantitative Trajectory Evaluation for Visual(-Inertial) Odometry (IROS 2018)

sections.title: Absolute error depends on the permitted alignment
body: For one run, define position error from the aligned estimate and associated reference. The equation below averages squared Euclidean position errors over K correspondences before taking the square root. Orientation error is a separate quantity, commonly the angle of the relative rotation; declare radians or degrees.

With observable metric scale and a common gravity frame, yaw plus translation removes the usual four global gauge freedoms of VIO. SE(3) also fits roll and pitch; Sim(3) additionally fits scale. Specify the allowed transform and fitting poses. The suitable policy depends on the estimator and motion assumptions, and each policy measures a different remaining error.

sources.title: OpenVINS: filter evaluation metrics
Zhang and Scaramuzza, A Tutorial on Quantitative Trajectory Evaluation for Visual(-Inertial) Odometry (IROS 2018)

sections.title: Relative error requires a pair convention
body: RPE compares estimated and reference relative motions for a specified set of pose pairs. Declare whether separation is measured in time, traveled distance, or frames, the interval and tolerance, and how starting poses and endpoints are selected. State whether distances come from the reference or estimate.

Report translation and rotation separately and name the statistic across pairs, such as median or RMSE. OpenVINS evaluation reports distance-segment RPE summaries; their pair counts differ from the number of trajectory poses. An error in meters is not a percentage drift, and an angle in degrees is not degrees per meter. Document any segment-length normalization.

sources.title: Zhang and Scaramuzza, A Tutorial on Quantitative Trajectory Evaluation for Visual(-Inertial) Odometry (IROS 2018)
OpenVINS: recording and evaluating estimator outputs

sections.title: Keep the levels of averaging explicit
body: OpenVINS distinguishes a trajectory RMSE for each run, a mean of run RMSEs, and a time-indexed RMSE across repeated runs. These answer different questions. Averaging sequence-level RMSEs is another level: it gives each contributing sequence equal weight unless a different weighting is specified.

The arithmetic mean of run RMSEs is generally different from pooling all squared pose errors and then taking one square root, even when runs contain equally many samples. Keep pose counts, RPE pair counts, contributing runs, and contributing sequences separate. Report the finite-value rule and missing contributors. This lesson defines the distinction; it does not change the historical VIOBench aggregation.

sources.title: OpenVINS: filter evaluation metrics

sections.equation: mean run RMSE = (1/R) Σ_r e_r; pooled pose RMSE = sqrt[Σ_r K_r e_r² / Σ_r K_r]

sections.title: Report evaluated extent and missing outcomes
body: A low error over the associated output does not establish accuracy over the entire recording. Report initialization, output gaps, final output time, eligible reference intervals, and attempted runs. In this lesson, matched-sample coverage means matched reference samples divided by eligible reference samples; a time fraction or completed-run fraction requires its own denominator.

EPICA also reports a local drift-valid path fraction. Its denominator follows the reference path supplied to that evaluation stage, after the selected association and preprocessing. Keep that fraction separate from missing-recording coverage and successful-run rate. Record the package version, selection rules, thresholds, and global-failure status. Public EPICA 0.1.17 and its live documentation differ in global-gate handling, so do not infer historical VIOBench rules from current documentation.

exercise.question: An estimate matches 800 of 1,000 eligible reference samples and has 0.05 m position RMSE on those matches. What can you report?
exercise.answer: Under this sample-based definition, matched-sample coverage is 80%, and position RMSE is 0.05 m over the 800 matches. This does not establish the error over the missing 200 samples or imply 80% time coverage.

title: Runtime and resource measurement
summary: Separate processing time, latency, throughput, and utilization when judging whether an estimator keeps up with its input.
objectives: Define the boundaries of a timing measurement
Compare a timing distribution with input cadence
Record enough platform information to interpret a result

sections.title: Define the operation and the processes measured
body: Processing time covers a named operation. Output latency spans a declared input event to a declared usable output, including any waiting inside that boundary. Throughput is completed work per unit time. Process CPU utilization and memory describe resource use; they are not interchangeable with elapsed processing time.

OpenVINS records timers inside VioManager separately from process resource polling. The upstream total spans its selected tracking, propagation, update, and marginalization work. Inspect the timer locations for the version used before including transport, decoding, visualization, or separate nodes in that total. Component intervals may overlap in other systems; adding them does not necessarily reconstruct a native total.

sources.title: OpenVINS: internal timings and process resource measurements
OpenVINS upstream: VioManager timer boundaries

sections.title: Compare distributions with input cadence
body: An illustrative 20 Hz camera stream has a 50 ms nominal interval. For stereo, define whether one processing event consumes a synchronized image pair. In a serial queue, sustained service slower than arrivals causes backlog unless inputs are dropped or throttled; concurrent processing requires measurements of the actual scheduling behavior.

Record mean, median, tail percentiles, and observed maximum, with the number of timed events and the included startup interval. Inspect queues, output latency, drops, and gaps. A mean below the input interval does not establish that every deadline is met. The observed maximum is limited to the measured run.

sources.title: OpenVINS: internal timings and process resource measurements

sections.title: Preserve resource and aggregation conventions
body: Record device, operating system, CPU/GPU, power and thermal conditions, thread settings, build options, source revision, input interval, resolution, camera mode, and estimator configuration. State which processes are included, the polling interval, CPU percentage convention, and the memory quantity and units. Resident memory, virtual memory, and device memory are different measurements.

CPU percentages on different devices do not express equal computational capacity. Also distinguish a time-sample average, a pooled-event average, and an equal-weight mean of run summaries. Retain run counts and missing values. These reporting requirements do not redefine the native total, CPU, or process-memory fields in the published VIOBench snapshot.

sources.title: OpenVINS: internal timings and process resource measurements

sections.title: Use profiling to investigate a measured cost
body: Internal timers identify expensive stages; a call-stack profiler helps locate work within them. Instrumentation changes runtime, so use profiled execution for diagnosis and repeat ordinary timing after a change. OpenVINS documents call-stack and memory profiling as separate developer workflows.

Keep the input, initialization outcome, estimated-trajectory extent, and accuracy checks alongside a speed comparison. Reducing processed frames, features, or state size can change both computational work and estimation quality. Report that changed condition with the measured result.

exercise.answer: No. The nominal interval is 50 ms, and some updates exceed it. Inspect queue behavior, output latency, and dropped inputs to determine whether the system catches up and meets the application's requirements.

title: Data acquisition and experimental setup
summary: Prepare an inspectable sensor recording, run a known configuration, and keep the evidence needed to diagnose and reproduce the result.
objectives: Check sensor content before tuning an estimator
Separate raw data, configuration, and generated outputs
Distinguish successful execution from demonstrated accuracy

sections.title: Inspect the sensor recording
body: Retain the raw recording unchanged. Check image encoding, resolution, camera ordering, shutter/exposure behavior, blur, and feature visibility. Inspect timestamp units, monotonicity, actual sample intervals, overlapping streams, and gaps. Verify gyroscope and accelerometer units and frame conventions; accelerometers report specific force, so a stationary sensor generally does not read zero on every axis.

Choose an initial test with understandable motion and a startup interval suitable for the selected initializer. Calibration data has a separate purpose: collect motion that excites the parameters being estimated while preserving image quality. Moderate motion alone is not a guarantee that every calibration parameter is observable.

sources.title: OpenVINS: camera and IMU calibration
Yang, Geneva, Zuo, and Huang, Online Self-Calibration for Visual-Inertial Navigation: Models, Analysis, and Degeneracy (T-RO 2023)

sections.title: Bind the recording to a supported sensor model
body: Provide the estimator with its supported camera model, intrinsics, spatial and temporal calibration, and IMU noise parameters. Verify transform direction, quaternion convention, and time-offset sign. Continuous-time noise density and discrete sample variance require different units and sampling-rate treatment. Image resizing or rectification must be reflected in the calibration and selected camera model.

OpenVINS separates estimator options, IMU properties, and camera–IMU calibration in its configuration files. Preserve launch-time overrides and enabled online-calibration states. The Yang et al. analysis explains why some motions leave parameters unobservable; enabling online calibration does not guarantee convergence or replace checking the initial calibration.

sections.title: Run an upstream baseline and retain the evidence
body: Reproduce a supported upstream example to check the installation, then change the recording and sensor configuration deliberately. Save the source revision, environment, exact command, resolved settings, input interval, initialization status, logs, and trajectory. Keep incomplete attempts in the run record with their observed outcome.

OpenVINS evaluation uses text beginning with time in seconds, position, and quaternion components qx qy qz qw. Declare position units, pose direction, physical frame, and whether output is online or revised later. Field order alone does not specify a quaternion multiplication convention or perform a sensor-frame conversion.

sections.title: State what the recording demonstrates
body: With suitable reference measurements, evaluate the common-frame trajectories under the declared association, alignment, and error conventions. Document reference quality and availability. A smooth plotted path alone establishes neither absolute accuracy nor a measured drift rate; reference-free checks can still expose gaps, implausible motion, timing problems, and inconsistent repeated behavior.

Save a short experiment record describing the sensor and calibration source, input identity, configuration, output type, attempted runs, evaluation settings, and known gaps. Make each reported number traceable to its input and output. Keep the installation check, successful initialization, completed execution, and demonstrated accuracy as distinct observations.

exercise.question: Your own recording produces a smooth trajectory but has no ground truth. What is a defensible first conclusion?
exercise.answer: The estimator produced the observed trajectory under the recorded configuration. Confirm initialization and completion from the logs, then report observed continuity and timing. A smooth plot without suitable reference measurements does not establish position accuracy or a measured drift rate.
